title: Why 'Dry Scooping' Pre-Workout Powder Is Sending Young People to the ER
excerpt: The TikTok-driven fitness trend of swallowing undiluted supplement powder has caused heart attacks, esophageal ulcers, and choking incidents — and one in five teen boys is trying it.
body:
• Dry scooping — consuming pre-workout powder without water — delivers the caffeine equivalent of two to three cups of coffee in a single concentrated hit, risking heart attacks, seizures, and respiratory failure.
  • A 20-year-old social media influencer suffered a heart attack after dry scooping, and a 25-year-old man required emergency coronary stent placement after three days of the practice.
  • A peer-reviewed study documented severe esophageal ulcers from dry scooping, with the undiluted powder causing chemical burns to the throat lining.
  • Research shows approximately one in five teen boys and young men have tried dry scooping, driven largely by social media fitness content.

What Dry Scooping Actually Does

The premise sounds simple enough: instead of mixing pre-workout supplement powder with water as directed, you dump a dry scoop directly into your mouth and swallow. Proponents on TikTok and fitness forums claim the undiluted dose delivers a faster, more intense energy boost before hitting the gym.

The reality is that dry scooping bypasses the gradual absorption that comes with drinking a diluted supplement. A typical pre-workout serving contains 91 to 387 milligrams of caffeine — the equivalent of one to three cups of coffee. When mixed with water and sipped over several minutes, the caffeine enters the bloodstream gradually. When swallowed as a concentrated powder, the entire dose hits at once.

The cardiovascular consequences can be immediate. Caffeine in high concentrations can cause rapid heart rate, heart palpitations, irregular heartbeat, and in severe cases, myocardial infarction — a heart attack.

The Case Reports

In 2021, 20-year-old Briatney Portillo, a social media influencer, suffered a heart attack after dry scooping pre-workout powder. She was otherwise healthy with no known cardiac conditions. The case drew widespread attention to the trend's dangers.

A peer-reviewed case study published in the medical literature documented a previously healthy 25-year-old man who presented with crushing chest pain after three days of dry scooping following a WhatsApp fitness group video. Emergency coronary angiography revealed a complete blockage of the proximal left anterior descending coronary artery — one of the heart's most critical vessels. He required emergency balloon angioplasty and a drug-eluting stent.

Another published study documented a patient who developed severe esophageal ulcers from dry scooping. The undiluted powder caused diffuse chemical burns to the throat lining, requiring proton pump inhibitor therapy and complete abstinence from the supplement for a four-week recovery period.

"Dry scooping could have a dangerous effect on your heart because high levels of caffeine might cause heart palpitations, an irregular heartbeat, or another cardiac problem. People who are more likely to participate in social media challenges are teens and 20-somethings who don't expect that copying something funny could threaten their well-being."

— Dr. Joseph Underwood, Chair of Emergency Medicine, Hackensack University Medical Center

Why Young People Are at Risk

The demographic most susceptible to the trend is also the most vulnerable to its effects. A recent study found that approximately one in five teen boys and young men have tried dry scooping. The behavior is driven almost entirely by social media — particularly TikTok fitness content where influencers demonstrate the practice.

Many young people who dry scoop do not realize they may have undiagnosed cardiac conditions. A person with an underlying heart issue may not experience symptoms during normal activity but could trigger a cardiac event with a concentrated caffeine dose. The risk compounds when dry scooping is combined with energy drinks or alcohol, both common in gym culture.

Pre-workout supplements are also not regulated by the FDA with the same rigor as pharmaceuticals. Their exact compositions and ingredient ratios can vary significantly between brands, making it difficult for users to know precisely how much caffeine and other stimulants they are consuming.

What Doctors Recommend

Medical professionals are unequivocal: always mix pre-workout supplements with the recommended amount of water. The dilution exists by design — it controls the rate of caffeine absorption and reduces the risk of choking or aspiration.

If someone tries dry scooping and develops chest pain, rapid heart rate, difficulty breathing, or sweating, they should seek emergency medical attention immediately. If symptoms are mild, the National Capital Poison Center recommends drinking water to clear residual powder and calling a poison control hotline for guidance.

The broader message from emergency medicine physicians is that fitness trends promoted on social media should not be treated as medical advice. A practice that sends healthy 20-somethings to the cardiac catheterization lab is not a shortcut to better workouts — it is a gamble with consequences that can be permanent.
